---
title: "Getting started"
subtitle: "A first project, end to end: add a paper, read it, make a plot, build the figure, cite both, export a PDF"
---

This walkthrough touches all five modes once, in the order a real project uses them. Twenty
minutes, one running example — a little growth-curve study. You'll need the app installed;
step 3 also uses the Python toolchain ([Installation](installation.qmd) covers both — and if
you don't have Python set up yet, you can skip step 3 and import any SVG or PNG you have lying
around instead).

# Create a project

Make a working folder for the study, then launch Flux and create a new project from the Home
screen — put it *inside* that folder and call it `paper`:

```
growth-study/          ← your working folder (analysis code will live here)
└── paper/             ← the Flux project you just created
```

A Flux project is [just a folder](concepts/projects-and-files.qmd) — everything you do from
here lands in readable files inside it. And notice what you won't do for the rest of this
tutorial: save. Flux [autosaves continuously](concepts/projects-and-files.qmd#saving-you-dont).

Working on two studies at once? Open a second window with **Ctrl+Shift+N** (also in your
taskbar's right-click menu on the Flux icon, or the New Window link on the Home screen) and
open the other project there. Each window holds one project; opening a project that's already
open in another window just focuses that window. You can also launch straight into a project
from a terminal: `flux ~/growth-study/paper`.

# Add a paper to your library

Open **Library** from the mode icons in the top bar. Paste a DOI into the add box at the top — any paper you
like, e.g. `10.1126/science.1070919` — and press Enter. The paper lands in
[your machine-global library](concepts/library-and-fluxlib.qmd), shared by every project.

Two buttons worth pressing now: **Enrich** (fills in the abstract, topics, and citation
counts) and the row's **⬇** (fetches an open-access PDF). Then click the row once — that
copies its citation key, which you'll paste into the manuscript in step 5.

# Read and mark it up

**Ctrl+Shift+click** the paper's row to open it in the **Reader**. Select an interesting
sentence — a color menu pops up; pick one and you've made a highlight. Click the highlight to
attach a note. Annotations anchor to the text itself and stay with the paper forever; the
Notes sidebar can export them all as Markdown whenever you want.
([More on the Reader.](modes/reader.qmd))

# Make a plot

Back in a terminal, set up the analysis environment in `growth-study/` and generate a plot
with [fluxplot](concepts/semantic-plots.qmd) — the library that makes plots *live* inside
Flux:

```bash
cd growth-study
uv init
uv add --editable ~/fluxplot
uv add cmasher numpy matplotlib
```

Save this as `make_growth.py`:

```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import fluxplot as fp
from fluxplot import style as fx
fx.use_light()

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
t = np.linspace(0, 24, 9)
control   = 0.05 * np.exp(0.28 * t) * rng.normal(1, 0.04, t.size)
treatment = 0.05 * np.exp(0.22 * t) * rng.normal(1, 0.04, t.size)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8))
fp.line(ax, t, control,   series="control",   marker="o", label="Control")
fp.line(ax, t, treatment, series="treatment", marker="s", label="Treatment")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (h)"); ax.set_ylabel("OD600")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.legend()
fx.despine(ax)
fx.title(ax, "Growth under nutrient stress", "control vs treatment")

fp.save(fig, "paper/plots/growth.svg",
        recipe=dict(script=__file__, params={}, inputs=[]))
```

```bash
uv run python make_growth.py
```

That wrote three files into the project's `plots/` — the plot, its parts manifest, and the
recipe to regenerate it. The two `series=` names are the handles everything downstream uses.

# Build the figure

Open **Figure** mode and press **Alt+I** — the importer lists `growth.svg` with a **◆
semantic** badge. Insert it: it lands at its true printed size (6.4 × 4.8 inches, exactly).

Now the trick that makes Flux Flux: **Ctrl+click** the control series' line. You've selected
one *part* of the plot. Press **F** and change its stroke color. That restyle is keyed to the
series name, so re-running `make_growth.py` later — different data, more points — updates the
plot in place *and keeps your styling*. Try **Alt+P** too: the X-ray shows the plot's whole
anatomy, and can regenerate it from its recipe.

Finish with a caption: **Alt+C** opens the caption editor beside the figure — write one
sentence and click back onto the canvas. ([More on Figure mode.](modes/figure.qmd))

# Write and cite

Open **Paper**. Write a sentence or two, then:

- Type `/figure` and pick your figure — it embeds as a chip with the live figure and your
  caption rendered beneath.
- Type `@@` to insert a reference to it ("Fig 1") in the prose. The number maintains itself.
- Type `@` and the first author's name of the paper from step 2 — pick it, and it becomes a
  citation chip; the bibliography updates itself. (Pasting a DOI straight into the text works
  too.)

([More on Paper mode.](modes/paper.qmd))

# Export

Click **Export** in the status bar and choose **PDF**. The manuscript renders with the figure,
its caption, the reference list — everything resolved — into the project's `exports/`.

Choosing **Word** offers one more thing: **Live Zotero citations**. Tick it and the
citations arrive in the `.docx` as real Zotero citations rather than as plain text, so
whoever opens it in Word can refresh them, change the citation style, renumber after an
edit, and add their own citations beside yours. Leave it unticked and the citations are
ordinary text, which is fine for a file nobody will edit.

Each citation travels with its full reference details, so it works on any machine, even
one that has never seen your library. If your co-author already sent you Word files
written with Zotero, **Link to library from…** takes those files and matches your
citations against the works in them, so the ones they already have arrive attached to
their own library entries instead of as separate copies — the dialog tells you how many
matched. Anything unmatched still works; it simply is not linked to anything.

# Encore: make it a slide

In Figure mode, the Inspector's **Send to deck…** turns your figure into a slide. Open
**Slide** mode, press **Animate ⏱**, select the plot and click **✨ Auto-animate** — then
**F5**. Your growth curves draw themselves onto the screen, beat by beat. **Export** here
produces a single `.html` file that plays the talk in any browser.
([More on Slide mode.](modes/slide.qmd))

# Where next

You've now seen the loop: read → plot → compose → write → cite → export, all in one folder.
From here:

- The five mode guides go deep on each workspace, with the
  [shortcut reference](reference/shortcuts.qmd) beside them.
- When the study grows, [regenerate plots instead of re-saving them](concepts/semantic-plots.qmd#regenerate-dont-re-save).
- And when you're ready for a collaborator who does the composing and citing *for* you, meet
  the [agent system](agents/collaboration.qmd): the same three steps you just did by hand are
  one instruction to `flux principal`.
